subject: Longitudinal data with a linear spline

messages.author: 9572ba991834d61e
messages.subject: Longitudinal data with a linear spline
parts:
I'm trying to fit a model with a non-linear trend for longitudinal data representing subjects that experience irreversible disease progression.  The data are normalized based on pre-diagnosis scores.

We assume that the diagnosis is not exact so the model includes a delta parameter that represents a time shift to adjust to when the disease may have actually begun.

Likewise, individuals may differ in where they begin prior to disease progression, so the model includes a vertical adjustment, gamma.

The model also includes a linear spline, and we want to constrain the parameters of the spline so that they reflect the fact that disease progression is irreversible.

I wrote up a model that I thought would work.  The first time I ran it, I didn't realize that I had mistakenly constrained the spline parameters in the opposite direction of the disease scores, but the Rhat values looked good so I was hopeful that it would work well when I flipped the direction of the spline parameters, but it totally bombed.  The Rhat values were large, and every one of the post-warmup samples had 'divergent transitions', which did not get fixed when I increased 'adapt_delta'.

I simulated data and ran that through and got similar results.  That code is here (I'm only fitting a few iterations while in the test phase and will greatly increase this when I feel comfortable that everything's working):

library(ggplot2)
library(rstan)
rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)
options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())

set.seed(1234)

# The timepoints are approximately continuous, so this is the error
errx <- rnorm(4000,0,0.1)

# The raw values for the time points without subject-level adjustment
rawx <- rep(-9:10,times=200)+errx

# Subject level adjustment for the time points
delta <- rnorm(200,0.5)

# The simulated time points
x <- rawx + rep(delta,each=20)

# Error for the results
erry <- rnorm(4000)

# Raw results without subject-level adjustment
rawy <- rep(c(0,0,0,0,0,0,0,0.4,1.3,2.3,3.8,5.3,6.8,8.3,9.8,10.8,11.3,11.1,11.5,11.8),times=200)+erry

# Subject level adjustment for the result
gamma <- rnorm(200,0,2)

# Simulated results
y <- rawy+rep(gamma,each=20)

simd <- data.frame(x,y,rawx,rawy,delta,gamma,subject=factor(rep(1:200,each=20)))

# The data that we have
ggplot(simd,aes(x=x,y=y,group=subject,color=subject))+
  geom_line()+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(legend.position="none")

# How we would like the data to look after adjustment
ggplot(simd,aes(x=rawx,y=rawy,group=subject,color=subject))+
  geom_line()+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(legend.position="none")

data_list <- list(N=4000, K=200, I=as.numeric(simd$subject), y=y, x=x)

model_code = '
data {
  int N; // Total number of observations
  int K; // Total number of subjects
  int I[N]; // Subject indicator
  vector[N] y; // Result
  vector[N] x; // Independent variable
}
parameters{
  real<lower=0> sigma; // Error variability
  positive_ordered[20] negalpha; // monotone non-decreasing
  vector[K] delta; // Horizontal subject-level shift
  vector[K] gamma; // Vertical subject-level shift
}
transformed parameters{
  vector[20] alpha;
  alpha <- -negalpha; // Switch to non-increasing
}
model {
  vector[N] shiftx;
  vector[N] funkx;
  int floorx[N];
  for(n in 1:N) {
    shiftx[n] <- x[n] - delta[I[n]]; // Horizontally shifted
    floorx[n] <- -10; // need to convert x to integer to index the alphas
    while ((floorx[n]+1) < floor(shiftx[n])) floorx[n] <- floorx[n] + 1;
    if (floorx[n] <= -10) { // create linear spline
      funkx[n] <- 0;
    } else if (floorx[n] >= 10) {
      funkx[n] <- alpha[20];
    } else {
      funkx[n] <- (1 - shiftx[n] + floorx[n])*alpha[floorx[n]+10] + (shiftx[n] - floorx[n])*alpha[floorx[n]+11];
    }
  }
  gamma ~ normal(0,1);
  delta ~ normal(0,2);
  negalpha ~ normal(0,10000);
  y ~ normal(gamma[I]+funkx,sigma);
}
'

# Compile the model
fit0 <- stan(model_code=model_code,data=data_list,chains=0)

# Sample the data with positive trend, even though the model is coded for a negative trend
sim1 <- stan(fit=fit0,data=data_list,warmup=10,iter=20)

# Flip the data so that it has a negative trend to match what the model expects
data_list2 <- list(N=4000, K=200, I=as.numeric(simd$subject), y=-y, x=x)
sim2 <- stan(fit=fit0,data=data_list2,warmup=10,iter=20)


My questions:
  1. I realize that it is fitting an awful lot of parameters, so I expect it to go slow, but is there anyway to get a speed boost?
  2. I'm using 'positive_ordered' to force monotonicity, but I suspect this may be causing problems.  Will it work like I want it to or should I do something else?
  3. Why does the model seem to work when my splines are constrained in the wrong direction and seem to break when they're going in the right direction?
  4. Is the following a better way to constrain the spline parameters (this time I'm forcing them to be non-decreasing instead of non-increasing)?  Is there a better way?

data {
    int N;
    int K;
    int I[N];
    vector[N] y;
    vector[N] x;
}
parameters{
  real<lower=0> sigma;
  vector[20] ralpha; // r is for random order
  vector[K] delta;
  vector[K] gamma;
}
transformed parameters{
  vector[20] aalpha; // a for absolute value
  vector[20] alpha;
  for(j in 1:20) aalpha[j] <- fabs(ralpha[j]); // take absolute value (forcing a half normal)
  alpha <- sort_asc(aalpha); // sort
}
model {
  vector[N] shiftx;
  vector[N] funkx;
  int floorx[N];
  for(n in 1:N) {
    shiftx[n] <- x[n] - delta[I[n]];
    floorx[n] <- -10;
    while ((floorx[n]+1) < floor(shiftx[n])) floorx[n] <- floorx[n] + 1;
    if (floorx[n] <= -10) {
      funkx[n] <- 0;
    } else if (floorx[n] >= 10) {
      funkx[n] <- alpha[20];
    } else {
      funkx[n] <- (1 - shiftx[n] + floorx[n])*alpha[floorx[n]+10] + (shiftx[n] - floorx[n])*alpha[floorx[n]+11];
    }
  }
  gamma ~ normal(0,1);
  delta ~ normal(0,2);
  ralpha ~ normal(0,10000);
  y ~ normal(gamma[I]+funkx,sigma);
}

Using the second model, I ran it with 4 chains of 100, with a warmup of 50.  I bumped max_treedepth up to 15.  When the data had a non-decreasing trend (which is what the model expects), all 200 post-warmup transitions exceeded the maximum treedepth and the Rhats varied from 6.8 to over 300.  On the other hand, when the data had a non-increasing trend (contrary to what the model expects), only about a quarter of the post-warmup transitions exceeded the maximum treedepth and all of the Rhats were less than 1.1 (usually around 1.02 and 1.03).

Why does it work better for data that are going in the wrong direction?!

> shiftx[n] <- x[n] - delta[I[n]]; // Horizontally shifted
> floorx[n] <- -10; // need to convert x to integer to index the alphas
> while ((floorx[n]+1) < floor(shiftx[n])) floorx[n] <- floorx[n] + 1;
> if (floorx[n] <= -10) { // create linear spline
> funkx[n] <- 0;
> } else if (floorx[n] >= 10) {
> funkx[n] <- alpha[20];
> } else {
> funkx[n] <- (1 - shiftx[n] + floorx[n])*alpha[floorx[n]+10] + (shiftx[n] - floorx[n])*alpha[floorx[n]+11];
> }
> }
> gamma ~ normal(0,1);
> delta ~ normal(0,2);
> negalpha ~ normal(0,10000);
> y ~ normal(gamma[I]+funkx,sigma);
> }
> '
>
> # Compile the model
> fit0 <- stan(model_code=model_code,data=data_list,chains=0)
>
> # Sample the data with positive trend, even though the model is coded for a negative trend
> sim1 <- stan(fit=fit0,data=data_list,warmup=10,iter=20)
>
> # Flip the data so that it has a negative trend to match what the model expects
> data_list2 <- list(N=4000, K=200, I=as.numeric(simd$subject), y=-y, x=x)
> sim2 <- stan(fit=fit0,data=data_list2,warmup=10,iter=20)
>
>
> My questions:
> • I realize that it is fitting an awful lot of parameters, so I expect it to go slow, but is there anyway to get a speed boost?

I don't think this model's going to work at all given the
way you're dealing with the splines. You lose derivative
information in the definition of funkx[], which is why we
didn't build in primitives to do what you're doing with loops.

Sometimes it can work despite broken Hamiltonians, but you
need to be very careful with simulations, as it looks like
your'e doing.

> • I'm using 'positive_ordered' to force monotonicity, but I suspect this may be causing problems. Will it work like I want it to or should I do something else?

positive_ordered is just constrained to give you a vector
(alpha[1], ..., alpha[K]) where 0 < alpha[1] < alpha[2] < ... < alpha[K].
I can't say what you want here.

> • Why does the model seem to work when my splines are constrained in the wrong direction and seem to break when they're going in the right direction?

I'm assuming that's a bug. You want to include print() statements,
etc., to test that the bits of your program are doing what you want them
to do.

> • Is the following a better way to constrain the spline parameters (this time I'm forcing them to be non-decreasing instead of non-increasing)? Is there a better way?

I couldn't really follow either approach.

- Bob

> int N;
> int K;
> int I[N];
> vector[N] y;
> vector[N] x;
> }
> parameters{
> real<lower=0> sigma;
> vector[20] ralpha; // r is for random order
> vector[K] delta;
> vector[K] gamma;
> }
> transformed parameters{
> vector[20] aalpha; // a for absolute value
> vector[20] alpha;
> for(j in 1:20) aalpha[j] <- fabs(ralpha[j]); // take absolute value (forcing a half normal)
> alpha <- sort_asc(aalpha); // sort
> }
> model {
> vector[N] shiftx;
> vector[N] funkx;
> int floorx[N];
> for(n in 1:N) {
> shiftx[n] <- x[n] - delta[I[n]];
> floorx[n] <- -10;
> while ((floorx[n]+1) < floor(shiftx[n])) floorx[n] <- floorx[n] + 1;
> if (floorx[n] <= -10) {
> funkx[n] <- 0;
> } else if (floorx[n] >= 10) {
> funkx[n] <- alpha[20];
> } else {
> funkx[n] <- (1 - shiftx[n] + floorx[n])*alpha[floorx[n]+10] + (shiftx[n] - floorx[n])*alpha[floorx[n]+11];
> }
> }
> gamma ~ normal(0,1);
> delta ~ normal(0,2);
> ralpha ~ normal(0,10000);
> y ~ normal(gamma[I]+funkx,sigma);
> }
>
>

>
> We assume that the diagnosis is not exact so the model includes a delta parameter that represents a time shift to adjust to when the disease may have actually begun.
>
> Likewise, individuals may differ in where they begin prior to disease progression, so the model includes a vertical adjustment, gamma.
>
> The model also includes a linear spline, and we want to constrain the parameters of the spline so that they reflect the fact that disease progression is irreversible.
>
> I wrote up a model that I thought would work.  The first time I ran it, I didn't realize that I had mistakenly constrained the spline parameters in the opposite direction of the disease scores, but the Rhat values looked good so I was hopeful that it would work well when I flipped the direction of the spline parameters, but it totally bombed.  The Rhat values were large, and every one of the post-warmup samples had 'divergent transitions', which did not get fixed when I increased 'adapt_delta'.
>
> I simulated data and ran that through and got similar results.  That code is here (I'm only fitting a few iterations while in the test phase and will greatly increase this when I feel comfortable that everything's working):
>
> library(ggplot2)
> library(rstan)
> rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)
> options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())
>
> set.seed(1234)
>
> # The timepoints are approximately continuous, so this is the error
> errx <- rnorm(4000,0,0.1)
>
> # The raw values for the time points without subject-level adjustment
> rawx <- rep(-9:10,times=200)+errx
>
> # Subject level adjustment for the time points
> delta <- rnorm(200,0.5)
>
> # The simulated time points
> x <- rawx + rep(delta,each=20)
>
> # Error for the results
> erry <- rnorm(4000)
>
> # Raw results without subject-level adjustment
> rawy <- rep(c(0,0,0,0,0,0,0,0.4,1.3,2.3,3.8,5.3,6.8,8.3,9.8,10.8,11.3,11.1,11.5,11.8),times=200)+erry
>
> # Subject level adjustment for the result
> gamma <- rnorm(200,0,2)
>
> # Simulated results
> y <- rawy+rep(gamma,each=20)
>
> simd <- data.frame(x,y,rawx,rawy,delta,gamma,subject=factor(rep(1:200,each=20)))
>
> # The data that we have
> ggplot(simd,aes(x=x,y=y,group=subject,color=subject))+
>   geom_line()+
>   theme_bw()+
>   theme(legend.position="none")
>
> # How we would like the data to look after adjustment
> ggplot(simd,aes(x=rawx,y=rawy,group=subject,color=subject))+
>   geom_line()+
>   theme_bw()+
>   theme(legend.position="none")
>
> data_list <- list(N=4000, K=200, I=as.numeric(simd$subject), y=y, x=x)
>
> model_code = '
> data {
>   int N; // Total number of observations
>   int K; // Total number of subjects
>   int I[N]; // Subject indicator
>   vector[N] y; // Result
>   vector[N] x; // Independent variable
> }
> parameters{
>   real<lower=0> sigma; // Error variability
>   positive_ordered[20] negalpha; // monotone non-decreasing
>   vector[K] delta; // Horizontal subject-level shift
>   vector[K] gamma; // Vertical subject-level shift
> }
> transformed parameters{
>   vector[20] alpha;
>   alpha <- -negalpha; // Switch to non-increasing
> }
> model {
>   vector[N] shiftx;
>   vector[N] funkx;
>   int floorx[N];
>   for(n in 1:N) {
>     shiftx[n] <- x[n] - delta[I[n]]; // Horizontally shifted
>     floorx[n] <- -10; // need to convert x to integer to index the alphas
>     while ((floorx[n]+1) < floor(shiftx[n])) floorx[n] <- floorx[n] + 1;
>     if (floorx[n] <= -10) { // create linear spline
>       funkx[n] <- 0;
>     } else if (floorx[n] >= 10) {
>       funkx[n] <- alpha[20];
>     } else {
>       funkx[n] <- (1 - shiftx[n] + floorx[n])*alpha[floorx[n]+10] + (shiftx[n] - floorx[n])*alpha[floorx[n]+11];
>     }
>   }
>   gamma ~ normal(0,1);
>   delta ~ normal(0,2);
>   negalpha ~ normal(0,10000);
>   y ~ normal(gamma[I]+funkx,sigma);
> }
> '
>

> fit0 <- stan(model_code=model_code,data=data_list,chains=0)
>
